findings.claim: More than 20 years ago, in December 2000, HCA subsidiaries pleaded guilty to criminal charges, and in 2001 subsidiary Columbia Management Companies pleaded guilty to false cost-report statements and a kickback conspiracy. In June 2003 the Justice Department put its recovery from HCA in fines, settlements and repayments at $1.7 billion, its largest in health care fraud; it names no Frist.

In November 2015 HCA agreed in principle to pay $215 million, without admitting wrongdoing, to settle a shareholder class action alleging its 2011 IPO documents failed to disclose declining revenue; a federal court in Tennessee approved it in April 2016. HCA estimated its net cost, with related derivative suits, at about $120 million after insurance.

In November 2006 HCA and the other named parties agreed, subject to court approval, to settle six consolidated purported class actions in a Tennessee court over the buyout of HCA by Bain Capital, KKR, Merrill Lynch and Thomas Frist Jr., with extra disclosure and a cap on the termination fee; the defendants denied the allegations. The release does not say whether Frist was a defendant.

North Carolina's attorney general sued HCA in December 2023, alleging it breached its 2019 purchase agreement for Mission Health by cutting emergency and cancer care; HCA says it complies. On 27 July 2026 the Business Court denied both sides' summary judgment motions, so the case goes to trial; no trial date had been reported.

In August 2025 HCA and Mission Health settled a 2022 antitrust suit by Brevard, Asheville, Buncombe County and Madison County alleging monopolistic tactics, agreeing to fund a $1 million charity fund and keep a Brevard hospital open to 2032. They denied the allegations; a Buncombe County suit over emergency-room staffing was still pending.

In Davis v. HCA, a 2021 class suit alleging HCA and Mission used market dominance to impose anticompetitive terms on insurers and raise premiums in western North Carolina, the Business Court denied class certification without prejudice on 8 September 2026. On 30 September it paused deadlines after the parties reported an agreement in principle on a class-wide settlement; terms were not public.

In October 2025 a federal court in Tennessee gave final approval to HCA's settlement of 27 consolidated suits over a 2023 data breach affecting more than 11 million patients; the total was not disclosed and HCA denied wrongdoing.

HCA reports that in 2025 it and its affiliates gave $450,000 to both parties' governors' associations and two Republican state-level groups, and paid $2.0 million in trade-association dues allocated to lobbying; in July to December 2025 they gave $4.2 million to state candidates, committees and PACs, about $3.0 million of it to HCA's own state PACs. No personal spending by Frist was found.

The Frist Foundation, a Nashville private foundation chaired by Patricia Frist Elcan, with Frist family directors and Thomas Frist Jr. as director emeritus (chairman on its 2013 to 2018 returns), reported charitable disbursements of $59.2 million in 2024 and $19.1 million in 2023 on its IRS 990-PF returns.

politics.reason: HCA reports ordinary corporate political activity: in 2025 it gave $450,000 to party groups of both parties and paid $2.0 million in trade-association dues allocated to lobbying, and in the second half of the year its affiliates gave $4.2 million to state candidates, committees and PACs, mostly HCA's own state PACs. No personal political spending by Thomas Frist Jr. was found.

In 2026 a private antitrust class suit was denied class status without prejudice, then a settlement was reported in principle.

results.comment: Rewritten: the DOJ release does not say what the December 2000 pleas were for; only the 2001 Columbia Management Companies pleas are false cost-report statements and kickback conspiracy. $1.7bn is what the government 'will have recovered' with the June 2003 settlements, not an amount already paid. Added that the events are over 20 years old. Frist is not named in the release.

Rewritten: the 8-K describes a preliminary agreement in principle (Nov 2015) without admission; Robbins Geller describes the claims as failure to disclose declining revenue in IPO documents, approved 14 April 2016 (M.D. Tenn.). $120m is HCA's estimate net of expected insurance.

Rewritten: a memorandum of understanding to settle 'purported' class actions, subject to court approval, not a completed settlement. Termination-fee waiver above $220m, supplemental disclosure and denial confirmed; the release names Frist as part of the buyout group.
WFAE (28 July 2026): Judge Earp denied both sides' motions to decide the case before trial on 27 July 2026; filed December 2023; no trial date given. A search on 2026-11-08 found no trial date since.
NC Health News: $1m charity fund, Transylvania Regional Hospital in Brevard kept open to at least 2032, allegations denied, Buncombe County ER-staffing suit pending.

Rewritten: both cited sources were law-firm pages (Simpson Thacher is HCA's counsel; Duane Morris a defence blog), so they were replaced with Asheville Watchdog reports. These show the 8 September 2026 denial was without prejudice, with a renewed motion invited, and that on 30 September the court paused deadlines after an agreement in principle on a class-wide settlement. Evidence type changed from final_ruling to pending_case.

GovInfoSecurity (31 Oct 2025): a Tennessee federal court approved the settlement of 27 consolidated suits over the 2023 breach (more than 11 million people); total not disclosed; HCA denies wrongdoing.

Rewritten: the $450,000 went to the DGA, RGA, RAGA and the Republican State Leadership Committee, not only governors' and AG groups. Of the $4,216,641 given in July to December 2025, about $3.0m went to HCA's own state PACs. Trade-association lobbying dues total $2,028,940.
